In [[nonlinear functional analysis]], the '''Krasnoselskii genus''' generalizes the notion of [[dimension]] for [[vector spaces]]. The Krasnoselskii genus of a linear space <math>A</math> is the smallest [[natural number]] <math>n</math> for which there exists a [[continuous function|continuous]] [[odd function]] of the form <math>f : A \to \R^n \setminus {0}</math>. The genus was introduced by [[Mark Krasnoselsky|Mark Aleksandrovich Krasnoselskii]] in 1964,<ref>{{cite book |last=Krasnoselskii |first=Mark A. |title=Topological Methods in the Theory of Nonlinear Integral Equations |year=1964 |publisher=Macmillan |location=New York |translator=A.H. Armstrong}}</ref> and an equivalent definition was provided by Charles Coffman in 1969.<ref name="Coffman">{{cite journal |last=Coffman |first=Charles V. |title=A minimum-maximum principle for a class of non-linear integral equations |journal=J. Analyse Math. |volume=22 |pages=391–419 |year=1969}}</ref>

== Krasnoselskii Genus ==
We follow the definition given by Coffman.<ref name="Coffman"/>

Let
*<math>E</math> be a [[Banach space]],
*<math>\mathcal{A} = \{A \subset E : A \text{ closed},; A = -A\}</math> be the collection of symmetric closed subsets of <math>E</math>,
*<math>C(A,\R^n)</math> the space of continuous functions <math>A \to \R^n</math>.

For <math>A \in \mathcal{A}</math> define the set
:<math>K_A =\{ n \in \N : \exists f \in C(A,\R^n \setminus {0}),; f(-x) = -f(x)\}</math>
Then the Krasnoselskii genus of <math>A</math> is defined as<ref>{{cite book |last=Struwe |first=Michael |title=Variational Methods: Applications to Nonlinear Partial Differential Equations and Hamiltonian Systems |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |year=2012 |pages=94}}</ref>
:<math>\gamma(A)=\begin{cases}\inf K_A &\text{if }K_A\neq \emptyset,\\
\infty &\text{if }K_A=\emptyset, \\
0 & \text{if } A=\emptyset.\end{cases}</math>

In other words, if <math>\gamma(A) = n</math> then there exists a continuous odd function <math>\varphi : A \to \R^n</math> such that <math>0 \notin \varphi(A)</math>. Moreover <math>n</math> is the minimal possible dimension, i.e. there exists no such function <math>\theta : A \to \R^d</math> with <math>d < n</math>.

=== Properties ===
* Let <math>\Omega \subset \R^n</math> be a bounded symmetric neighborhood of <math>0</math> in <math>\R^n</math>. Then the genus of its boundary is <math>\gamma(\partial \Omega) = n</math>.<ref>{{cite book |last=Struwe |first=Michael |title=Variational Methods: Applications to Nonlinear Partial Differential Equations and Hamiltonian Systems |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |year=2012 |pages=95}}</ref>
* For <math>A, B \in \mathcal{A}</math>, the following holds:<ref>{{cite book |last=Ambrosio |first=Vincenzo |title=Nonlinear Fractional Schrödinger Equations in \mathbb{R}^N |location=Germany |publisher=Springer International Publishing |year=2021 |pages=43}}</ref>
# If there exists an odd function <math>f \in C(A, B)</math>, then <math>\gamma(A) \leq \gamma(B)</math>.
# If <math>A \subset B</math>, then <math>\gamma(A) \leq \gamma(B)</math>.
# If there exists an odd [[homeomorphism]] between <math>A</math> and <math>B</math>, then <math>\gamma(A) = \gamma(B)</math>.

Combining these statements, it follows immediately that if there exists an odd homeomorphism between <math>A</math> and <math>\partial \Omega</math> then <math>\gamma(A) = n</math>.
